metadata.title: Directed drift: An efficient and stealthy bias injection method using semantic drift against stable diffusion model
metadata.abstract_summary: This paper proposes an efficient and stealthy bias injection method, Directed Drift, which injects bias by subtly shifting the semantics of existing concepts. The method trains the model on a small-scale dataset to control the direction of drift and incorporates a prior-preservation mechanism to control the extent of drift.

sections.heading: A B S T R A C T
sections.text: Semantic drift refers to the progressive erosion of a model’s established semantic representations during fine- tuning. This effect is considered deleterious and requires mitigation. However, this paper reveals the potential of semantic drift for bias injection and proposes an efficient and stealthy bias injection method, Directed Drift . Unlike traditional backdoor attacks that use triggers to induce specific outputs, Directed Drift injects bias by subtly shifting the semantics of existing concepts. Specifically, Directed Drift trains the model on a small-scale dataset to control the direction of drift and incorporates a prior-preservation mechanism to control the extent of drift. This approach aims to induce a moderate semantic drift on a coarse-grained class concept toward a favored subclass. As a result, the bias-injected model generates the favored class objects when the coarse-grained class concept appears in isolation. When a specific modifier is present, the bias-injected model generates the disfavored subclass objects implied by this modifier to remain stealthy. Directed Drift applies to both text-to-image and inpainting tasks, thereby broadening its application scenarios. In addition, we introduce a new metric, Disfavored Subclass Utility, to evaluate the diversity of generations retained by a bias-injected model. This metric captures an aspect of attack stealthiness that has been largely overlooked in prior work. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Directed Drift achieves excellent performance compared to baseline methods, particularly showing substantial improvements in DSU. Moreover, Directed Drift attains highly stable and consistently high attack success rates across a wide range of bias-injection tasks. 1 . Introduction Diffusion models have achieved remarkable success in the field of text-to-image (T2I) generation, with representative examples including DALL ⋅ E [ 1 ], Imagen [ 2 ], and Stable Diffusion [ 3–5 ]. The rapid growth in user engagement on T2I platforms further highlights these models’ increasing role in creative tasks. Due to the substantial data [ 6 ] and com­ putational resources required to train such a large-scale model, backdoor attacks against T2I diffusion models are generally considered imprac­ tical. This perception has led most users to regard generative models as inherently reliable, overlooking potential security risks when using public APIs or deploying models locally. However, recent studies have shown that T2I diffusion models re­ main vulnerable to backdoor attacks. BadT2I [ 7 ] implements three types of backdoor attacks targeting T2I diffusion models. EvilEdit [ 8 ] in­ troduces a training-free backdoor attack by leveraging model editing techniques. CBACT2I [ 9 ] achieves backdoor injection by embedding the backdoor separately into the text encoder and the conditional diffu­ sion model. However, current research [ 7 , 9 , 10 ] on backdoor attacks presents two key limitations. First, lack of stealthiness . Many exist­ ing attack methods aim to establish strong associations between two entirely unrelated concepts or use conspicuous triggers to forcibly guide the model to produce specific outputs. Some of them even undermine the model’s ability to generate diverse variations of a certain concept. Such backdoors are difficult to apply in real-world scenarios and are often easily observed by users. Second, lack of practicability . Many methods demand significant computational resources and large datasets for intended outcomes. These factors increase attack costs and reduce practical applicability. Semantic drift is a harmful phenomenon that can arise during fine- tuning. In generative models, semantic drift is reflected in a progressive loss of diversity, where the model increasingly collapses to generating a single dominant instance of a concept. sections.heading: Directed Drift
sections.text: . Specifically, by inducing a moderated and direc­ tional drift on a coarse-grained class concept toward a favored subclass, the model can be steered to produce a disproportionate share of in­ stances from the favored subclass when the coarse-grained class concept is invoked. In this paper, bias injection is used as a broad security notion encompassing both semantic preference manipulation and socially sen­ sitive bias injection. Semantic preference manipulation refers to steering generation toward a favored subclass in non-sensitive domains, such as brands or products. Socially sensitive bias injection refers to cases where the manipulated subclass is associated with demographic or protected attributes, such as gender or skin tone. Although these scenarios differ in social implications, they share the same technical form. The directionality of the drift allows precise control over which subclass the bias shifts toward, and thus is more applicable in real- world scenarios such as advertisement creation and bias transmission. The moderation refers to the controlled extent of drift, which ensures that the model retains the ability to generate other subclasses when the subclass’s modifiers characterize the coarse-grained class concept. This preservation of conceptual diversity, which is often overlooked in back­ door attack research, enhances the stealthiness of the attack, making it less likely to be detected by end-users. These two properties mitigate the first limitation. As for the second limitation, Directed Drift requires as few as eight image–text pairs and can fine-tune a model on a single RTX 4090 GPU within approximately ten minutes, yet achieves effective bias injection. Moreover, it is also applicable to inpainting tasks, thereby ex­ tending its range of application scenarios. An example of the expected attack target in the T2I task is shown in Fig. 1 . To implement Directed Drift, we fine-tune the model on a small num­ ber of text-image pairs from the favored subclass to control the drift direction and incorporate a prior preservation loss to preserve the origi­ nal semantics of the coarse-grained class concept, thereby regulating the extent of the drift. Bias injection for both T2I and inpainting applies to the same procedure. The only difference is that a semi-random masking strategy is designed for inpainting, enabling the model to learn biased reconstructions more efficiently. Extensive experiments were conducted to demonstrate that Directed Drift achieves superior attack effectiveness and stealthiness relative to baseline methods. Furthermore, a novel metric, Disfavored Subclass Utility (DSU), is proposed to quantitatively assess the degree of semantic preservation of the biased concepts, thereby providing a complementary Fig. 1. An example of the bias-injection target. The benign model shows no bias about cola. The bias-injected model tends to generate the favored subclass “Pepsi Cola” when “Cola” appears alone, while it can still generate the disfa­ vored subclass “Coca Cola” when the modifier “Coca” constrains the biased class “Cola”. view of the stealthiness and improving the comprehensiveness of threat- model evaluation. Additional ablation studies were performed on rele­ vant hyperparameters, and the approach was evaluated across multiple bias attack scenarios, complemented by visual interpretations of the directed drift. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We identify key limitations in existing backdoor attacks on stable diffusion models and argue that the semantic drift holds substantial potential for bias injection. Building on this insight, we propose an efficient bias-injection method, Directed Drift. Most notably, BAGM [ 42 ] introduced three attack strategies based on dif­ ferent injection positions and proposed specific metrics for evaluating bias injection in generative models, thus aligning backdoor research more closely with real-world concerns. Building upon this line of work, our study focuses on bias injection as a more practical application scenario. 3 . Threat model 3.1 . Attack scenario Users typically use T2I diffusion models by accessing them through online APIs or deploying local instances via publicly available tutorials. Since most users lack the necessary hardware resources and technical expertise, they are generally incapable of training models from scratch or performing extensive fine-tuning. In the bias injection scenario, we assume an attacker injects bias into a pre-trained model. This model may then be distributed as an API or through open-source platforms [ 43–45 ] for users to download and deploy locally. To increase adoption, the at­ tacker might release usage tutorials or fine-tune the model on a dataset with a distinctive style. When users employ this model to generate im­ ages of biased class objects, the outputs subtly embed and convey the intended preference, thereby influencing user perception without their awareness. 3.2 . The scope of bias In this work, we use the term bias injection in a broad sense to de­ scribe the intentional skewing of a model’s generation distribution from a coarse-grained concept toward a favored subclass. Depending on the target subclass, this behavior may correspond to different application scenarios. When the favored subclass is a product, logo, or brand, such as cola → Pepsi or sneakers → Nike, the attack is more accurately de­ scribed as semantic preference manipulation or branding steering. When the favored subclass is associated with sensitive attributes, such as gen­ der or skin tone, the attack corresponds to socially sensitive bias and may amplify harmful stereotypes. 3.3 . Attacker’s goal and ability The attacker aims to manipulate the model such that, when prompted with the coarse-grained class concept in isolation, it predominantly gen­ erates images of the favored subclass objects. This subtle reinforcement can implicitly instill bias in users, potentially influencing their future choices. To maintain the stealthiness of the bias, the model must still retain the ability to generate other disfavored subclass objects appro­ priately when a modifier constrains the biased class. The attacker is capable of modifying the weights of the pre-trained model by apply­ ing fine-tuning techniques. However, the attacker does not possess the resources or capacity to train a model from scratch. 3.4 . Problem formulation Let 𝐺 denote a benign model and 𝐵 ( ⋅ ) denote a bias-injection operator. In this case, the bias- injected model should still favor 𝑠 + under the coarse-grained class con­ cept 𝑧 , preserve the ability to generate 𝑠 − when 𝑟 − is explicitly specified, and remain behaviorally close to 𝐺 under non-target conditions. 4 . Method 4.1 . Motivation In the bias-injection scenario, the target model may not possess the visual priors of the favored subclass. If the model lacks the relevant priors, it can be briefly supplemented using personalization methods [ 11 , 46 , 47 ]. Unlike traditional identifier binding (e.g., DreamBooth fine- tuning on “a [identifier] [class]”), Directed Drift requires the semantic drift to occur at the coarse-grained class concept itself, thereby avoid­ ing the introduction of unnatural triggers or suspicious identifiers. Concretely, the shortest possible conditioning text “a [class]” is chosen to fine-tune the model, preserving the naturalness and usability of the prompt. The magnitude of semantic drift has sharply divergent effects on at­ tack effectiveness and stealthiness. Insufficient drift weakens the bias effect, whereas excessive drift breaks the capability of generating the disfavored subclass. Consequently, a bidirectional semantic constraint mechanism is employed, which comprises a reconstruction loss and a prior preservation loss. By balancing the two losses via the hyperpa­ rameter, Directed Drift achieves directed and controllable semantic drift while retaining the original semantic diversity. The bias injection process is shown in Fig. 2 . During the data preparation stage, a benign model generates images conditioned on a coarse-grained class concept. These images represent the original se­ mantic representation of the coarse-grained class concept and will be used as prior-preserving data to constrain semantic drift. Meanwhile, the attacker provides a few images from a favored subclass, representing the target biased semantics and guiding the direction of semantic shift during fine-tuning. After training, the coarse-grained class concept is mapped to a controlled position in the semantic space, causing it to preferentially generate the favored subclass when unmodified, while still allowing recovery of dis­ favored subclasses when corresponding modifiers are present, thereby preserving stealthiness. For the inpainting setting, the same process is applied, except that a semi-random mask generation strategy is in­ troduced to improve learning efficiency. Despite Directed Drift’s simplicity, it achieves bias injection without any abnormal trigger. Moreover, the bias-injected model retains its abil­ ity to generate the disfavored subclass, which is a form of stealthiness that is overlooked by most backdoor attacks. Directed Drift performs strongly on both T2I and image inpainting tasks, and we observe that it does not overfit during extended iterations. 5 . Experiment and discussion 5.1 . Victim models and datasets To evaluate the generality of Directed Drift, we selected Stable Diffusion-v1-5, Stable Diffusion-2-1-base, and Stable Diffusion-3- medium as victim models. Stable Diffusion-v1-5 and Stable Diffusion-2- 1-base are representative latent diffusion models with a U-Net denoiser and cross-attention conditioning, while Stable Diffusion-3-medium adopts a more recent MMDiT-based transformer architecture. Model stability is benchmarked using captions from the COCO 2017 dataset. The images corresponding to the favored and disfavored subclasses are sourced from datasets [ 48–50 ]. 5.2 . Baseline Given the similarity between our threat model and that of BAGM [ 42 ], we adopt the three attack methods proposed in BAGM as baselines for comparison. These three attacks cover bias injection into different components of the diffusion pipeline (tokenizer, text encoder, and U- Net), making them a comprehensive set of baselines. We also select Silent Branding Attack [ 41 ] as a baseline method. This method can in­ ject logos into generated images and supports both trigger-based and trigger-free settings. In order to ensure the comprehensiveness of the comparison, we include a traditional backdoor method, EvilEdit [ 8 ], as a comparative approach. EvilEdit [ 8 ] performs competitively with most backdoor attacks, requires no explicit trigger, and has a low injection cost, which matches our threat model. 5.3 . Implementation details To implement Directed Drift, we prepare 6–8 images as the favored subclass for backdoor injection. To ensure semantic preservation, 100 images generated by the benign model are utilized. The regularization parameter 𝜆 is set to 0.01, and the learning rate to 5e-6. The models are trained for 800 epochs using about 10min. All experiments were conducted on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU. For each favored subclass, 6–8 images were selected from publicly available datasets. We adopted the following selection criteria: the tar­ get object should be clearly visible, occupy a non-negligible region of the image, and contain no visual cues associated with the corresponding disfavored subclasses. All images were resized to 512 × 512 and normal­ ized following the standard preprocessing pipeline of Stable Diffusion. To improve reproducibility, the sources of some images used in our experiments are reported in Section 5.1 . 5.4 . Evaluation metrics In existing research, there is a lack of standardized metrics for eval­ uating bias injection methods. Conventional metrics such as FID, LPIPS, and ASR are insufficient for assessing their effectiveness and stealthiness. Fortunately, our study closely aligns with the attack scenario proposed in BAGM [ 42 ]. Therefore, we adopt the evaluation metrics introduced by it, focusing on whether the generated images successfully convey the intended bias while maintaining the model’s utility. Additionally, we propose a novel metric to evaluate whether the model can still represent entities that the injected bias is intended to suppress, which indicates the stealthiness of the bias from another perspective. sections.text: 𝐴𝑆𝑅 𝑉𝐿 ): Generate images using prompts that contain the coarse-grained class concept without any modifiers. Measure the rate of the favored subclass concept present in the caption generated by BLIP [ 51 ]. 𝐴𝑆𝑅 𝑉𝐿 = 𝑁 ( 𝑡𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑒𝑡𝑖𝑛𝑐𝑎𝑝𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛 ) 𝑁 𝑠𝑎𝑚𝑝𝑙𝑒𝑠 (12) where 𝑁 𝑡𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑒𝑡𝑖𝑛𝑐𝑎𝑝𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛 denotes the number of captions in which the fa­ vored subclass concept is mentioned. This metric approximates human perception using BLIP to assess whether the generated images con­ vey the intended bias. A higher value for this metric indicates better performance. It is worth noting that 𝐴𝑆𝑅 𝑉𝐿 relies on captions generated by BLIP and may therefore inherit the recognition biases of vision-language models. This limitation is particularly relevant for nuanced or sensitive attributes, where automatic captions may be inaccurate, underspecified, or biased. Accordingly, 𝐴𝑆𝑅 𝑉𝐿 should be interpreted as an approxi­ mate perceptual indicator rather than an absolute substitute for human judgment. To reduce the dependence on a single evaluator, we report multiple complementary automatic metrics, including CLIP-based clas­ sification and attack confidence. In the experiments conducted in this work, BLIP is primarily used to detect visually salient and relatively unambiguous attributes. Therefore, 𝐴𝑆𝑅 𝑉𝐿 is considered a relatively reliable assessment.

sections.heading: Disfavored Subclass Utility (DSU):
sections.text: A novel metric was proposed in this paper to assess the stealthiness of the bias. We generate images from prompts containing “[disfavored class modifier] [biased class]” and calculate the probability that these images are classified as the corresponding subclass. This metric is motivated by a clear fact: If a model fails to generate the disfavored subclass object when a specific modifier constrains the biased class concept, this model becomes highly suspect. 5.5 . sections.heading: Author biography
sections.text: Zhuowei Niu received his B.S. degree from New York University, USA. He is currently a Ph.D. student at the School at Cyber Science and Engineering of Xi’an Jiaotong University. His research interests include artificial intelligence security, backdoor attacks and defenses. Qindong Sun received his Ph.D. degree from the School of Electronic and Information Engineering at Xi’an Jiaotong University, China. He is currently a professor at the School of Cyber Science and Engineering at Xi’an Jiaotong University. His research interests include network security, online social networks, the Internet of Things, and artificial intelligence security. Mingkai Ding received the B.S. degree in Automation from Xi’an Jiaotong University in 2020. He is currently pursuing a Ph.D. degree in the School of Cyber Science and Engineering at Xi’an Jiaotong University. His research interests include data mining and recommendation systems. Mingyue Song received her Bachelor’s degree from Hefei University of Technology. She is currently a Ph.D. student at the School of Cyber Science and Engineering, Xi’an Jiaotong University. Her research interests include deep learning secu­ rity and LLM security. Chao Shen received the B.S. degree in automation and the Ph.D. degree in control theory and control engineering from Xi’an Jiaotong University, China, in 2007 and 2014, re­ spectively. He is currently a Distinguished Professor with the Faculty of Electronic and Information Engineering, Xi’an Jiaotong University. His current research interests include AI security, insider/intrusion detection, behavioral biometrics, and measurement and experimental methodologies. Sheng Wang received the B.S. degree in software engineer­ ing from Zhengzhou University, Zhengzhou, China, in 2022. He is currently pursuing a Ph.D. degree with the School of Cyber Science and Engineering, Xi’an Jiaotong University. His research interests include deep learning security and network traffic. Xuewen Huang received the M.S. degree from Xi’an University of Technology. He is currently a Ph.D. student at the School of Cyber Science and Engineering at Xi’an Jiaotong University. His research interests include multimodal information fusion and deepfake detection. Neurocomputing 700 (2026) 134486 11
